evidence.excerpt: Modern assembly lines frequently switch between product variants, requiring inspection systems that adapt rapidly to new normal-appearance distributions without collecting defect examples in advance. This paper presents an adaptive one-class contrastive learning framework for unsupervised anomaly detection in multi-product settings. The approach uses a momentum-updated reference encoder and an online memory bank of normal embeddings that is refreshed at product changeover events, enabling the model to track appearance shifts without full retraining. A self-supervised pretext task based on synthetic local masking strengthens the encoder's sensitivity to subtle textural and structural anomalies. The framework is evaluated on a novel multi-variant industrial benchmark—PolyAssembly-7—covering seven polymer component types across four product families. It achieves an average AUROC of 93.1% across all variants and demonstrates adaptation in fewer than 50 unlabeled normal samples per changeover, outperforming five established one-class detection baselines. Inference runs at 28 fps on an NVIDIA Jetson edge module. The results highlight the viability of continual anomaly detection for flexible manufacturing without persistent human annotation effort.
